rationale: US20070237786A1 places Russian tarragon extract in a multi-ingredient proposed diet supplement. The tarragon discussion cites toxicology, glucose and sedative sources and supplies no isolated dried-herb fatigue outcome.
US20060286183A1 is a related formulation application naming Russian tarragon extract. Its fatigue language concerns the blend and components, with no ingredient-specific Parkinson fatigue comparison.
Canadian publication CA2550272A1 covers a related multiple-ingredient formulation. It supplies no controlled measurement of fatigue following dried tarragon.
WO2006133549A2 is a related disclosure centered on a Hoodia blend. Russian tarragon is among the compounds, with no separate culinary tarragon fatigue comparison.
Knaapila spice panel includes marjoram as a recognition stimulus and associates reported use with familiarity and recognition. It cannot establish change in Parkinson olfaction after dried herb.

Fifteen healthy participants chewed five flavored products. Spearmint flavor reached 4.03 mL/min at six minutes against 0.85 before chewing. Overall flavor comparison at six minutes was inconclusive. No unflavored control, dried leaf or drooling outcome.

Earlier report from an overlapping team uses the same volunteer count, schedule and flavors. All flavors stimulated saliva. It reports an early peak for all flavors and no significant late flavor differences. Possible overlap and differing peak descriptions are recorded.
Randomized spearmint-flavored gum and gum-base crossover in 12 adults found greater flow early with gum and later with base. Flavor composition and oral loss are unmeasured.
Liver disease narrative review discusses antioxidative compounds, including allyl isothiocyanate, without a toasted mustard seed postural control experiment.

Stress-model mouse experiment used inhaled isolated l-perillaldehyde. Experimental anosmia prevented its forced-swim effect. Olfactory recovery was not an outcome and dried shiso was not administered.
